claims.text: What the strip looks like Horizontal or downsloping ST depression ≥ 0.5 mm (subendocardial ischemia), or deep symmetric T-wave inversion (ischemia or post-ischemic).
claims.quote: ST depression (horizontal or downsloping, ≥ 0.5 mm): subendocardial ischemia T-wave inversion (symmetric, deep): ischemia or post-ischemic

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) ST depression: horizontal or downsloping, ≥ 0.5 mm at the J point in ≥ 2 contiguous leads (2007 Task Force criteria)
claims.quote: Horizontal or downsloping ST depression ≥ 0.5 mm at the J-point in ≥ 2 contiguous leads indicates myocardial ischaemia (according to the 2007 Task Force Criteria).

claims.text: ≥ 1 mm is more specific with a worse prognosis; ≥ 2 mm in ≥ 3 leads: high probability of NSTEMI, 35% mortality at 30 days
claims.quote: ST depression ≥ 1 mm is more specific and conveys a worse prognosis. ST depression ≥ 2 mm in ≥ 3 leads is associated with a high probability of NSTEMI and predicts significant mortality (35% mortality at 30 days).

claims.text: Upsloping ST depression: non-specific for ischemia
claims.quote: Upsloping ST depression is non-specific for myocardial ischaemia.

claims.text: T-wave inversion: may count as ischemic if ≥ 1 mm deep, in ≥ 2 continuous leads with dominant R waves, and dynamic; it is a normal variant in III, aVR and V1
claims.quote: T wave inversion may be considered to be evidence of myocardial ischaemia if: At least 1 mm deep Present in ≥ 2 continuous leads that have dominant R waves (R/S ratio > 1) Dynamic — not present on old ECG or changing over time NB. T wave inversion is only significant if seen in leads with upright QRS complexes (dominant R waves). T wave inversion is a normal variant in leads III, aVR and V1.

claims.text: Distribution: subendocardial ischemia is usually widespread (typically I, II, V4–6 and others)
claims.quote: ST depression due to subendocardial ischaemia is usually widespread — typically present in leads I, II, V4-6 and a variable number of additional leads.

claims.text: ST depression limited to one territory (especially inferior or high lateral) is more likely reciprocal to a STEMI — look for subtle ST elevation
claims.quote: ST depression localised to a particular territory (esp. inferior or high lateral leads only) is more likely to represent reciprocal change due to STEMI. The corresponding ST elevation may be subtle and difficult to see, but should be sought.

claims.text: Dynamic changes on serial EKGs carry more weight than a single tracing
claims.quote: Dynamic changes on serial EKGs carry more weight than a single tracing

claims.text: Mimics: e.g., LVH, digoxin effect — but dynamic ST and T changes strongly suggest ischemia
claims.quote: While there are numerous conditions that may simulate myocardial ischaemia (e.g. left ventricular hypertrophy, digoxin effect), dynamic ST segment and T wave changes (i.e. different from baseline ECG or changing over time) are strongly suggestive of myocardial ischaemia.

claims.text: Causes (mechanism and diagnoses) NSTEACS: NSTEMI or unstable angina — usually told apart afterwards by cardiac enzymes at 8–12 hours; same ECG changes and symptoms, managed the same in the ED
claims.quote: Non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome (NSTEACS) encompasses two main entities: Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI). Unstable angina pectoris (UAP). The differentiation between these two conditions is usually retrospective, based on the presence/absence of raised cardiac enzymes at 8-12 hours after the onset of chest pain. Both produce the same spectrum of ECG changes and symptoms and are managed identically in the Emergency Department.

claims.text: NSTEMI: myocardial necrosis (raised troponin) without acute ST elevation; usually not transmural
claims.quote: Non–ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI, subendocardial MI) is myocardial necrosis (evidenced by elevated cardiac troponin in blood) without acute ST-segment elevation. ECG changes such as ST-segment depression, T-wave inversion, or both may be present. NSTEMI is usually not transmural

claims.text: An abnormal troponin is the main thing separating unstable angina from MI, particularly without ST elevation
claims.quote: An abnormal cTn level, using an appropriate cutoff, is the primary distinguishing factor between unstable angina and myocardial infarction, particularly when ST elevation is not present.

claims.text: Symptoms The same as in STEMI
claims.quote: Symptoms of NSTEMI and STEMI are the same.
claims.locator: Symptoms and Signs of Acute MI

claims.text: Treatment Unstable (shock, ongoing symptoms, hypotension, sustained arrhythmias): straight to the cath lab for angiography
claims.quote: Patients with unstable NSTE-ACS (including NSTEMI and unstable angina) (ie, those with shock, ongoing symptoms, hypotension, or sustained arrhythmias) should be taken directly to the cardiac catheterization laboratory for angiography to identify coronary lesions requiring PCI or coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) (4).

claims.text: Uncomplicated NSTEMI: typically angiography within 24–72 hours
claims.quote: For patients with uncomplicated NSTEMI, reperfusion is not as urgent because a completely occluded infarct-related artery at presentation is uncommon. Such patients typically undergo angiography within the first 24 to 72 hours of hospitalization to identify coronary lesions requiring PCI or CABG (4).
